question: The Indus Valley Civilisation is also known by which of the following names?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bronze Age Civilisation.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Indus Valley Civilisation is also called the Bronze Age Civilisation because its people used bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, for tools, weapons and ornaments, while iron was completely unknown to them (कांस्य युगीन सभ्यता)

 

• It was India's first civilisation and, unlike the earlier village cultures, an urban civilisation, that is, a civilisation of planned cities with streets, drains and public buildings.

 

• The notes date the civilisation to about 2500-1750 BCE, and the economy rested mainly on wheat and barley cultivation supported by trade and craft production.

 

• The label 'Bronze Age' is a technological label; it tells us the metal stage of the culture, which is why options such as Iron Age or Megalithic are wrong for this civilisation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• It is equally known as the Harappan Civilisation, named after Harappa, the first site to be discovered.

 

• Iron came into regular use in the Ganga plain only around 1000 BCE with the Painted Grey Ware phase, centuries after the Harappan cities declined.

 

• The Neolithic (New Stone Age) and the Chalcolithic (copper-stone) phases came before the mature urban phase in the subcontinent.

 

• Two classic negative facts for SSC: no temple has been found and the script is still undeciphered.

 

NOTE

 

• Iron Age Civilisation (Option 1): The Iron Age belongs to a much later period in India; the Harappans did not know iron, so calling their civilisation an Iron Age one would be a factual error and it is the commonest trap in this question.

 

• Neolithic Civilisation (Option 2): Neolithic refers to the New Stone Age, marked by polished stone tools, early farming and pottery. The Harappans were a metal-using urban people, so this label describes an earlier, village-based stage instead.

 

• Megalithic Civilisation (Option 3): Megalithic denotes cultures that raised large stone burial monuments, mainly in peninsular India during the Iron Age. It is a much later phenomenon and has no link with the Harappan cities or their bronze technology.

question: Who was the first scholar to use the term 'Indus Valley Civilisation' (IVC)?
solution_text:
The correct answer is John Marshall.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• John Marshall, Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India (1902-1928), was the first scholar to use the term Indus Valley Civilisation (IVC) for the culture revealed at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro (सिंधु घाटी सभ्यता — जॉन मार्शल)

 

• It was Marshall who sent Daya Ram Sahani to the Sindhu (Indus) region in 1921, and this assignment led to the excavation of Harappa on the Ravi river.

 

• The announcement of the finds by Marshall in 1924 showed that India had an ancient urban civilisation contemporary with Mesopotamia and Egypt.

 

• Marshall also gave the seated, horned figure on the Mohenjo-daro seal the name Proto-Shiva (Pasupati), which is another frequently asked association with his name.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Alexander Cunningham, the first Director-General of ASI (1861), had seen a Harappan seal but never understood its antiquity.

 

• Harappa was excavated by Daya Ram Sahani in 1921 and Mohenjo-daro by R. D. Banerjee in 1922.

 

• Chanhudaro was found by N. G. Majumdar in 1931.

 

• The civilisation is also called Harappan after the first discovered site, as the PYQ on this theme confirms.

 

NOTE

 

• Alexander Cunningham (Option 2): Cunningham was the first head of the Archaeological Survey of India and came across a Harappan seal, but he did not recognise its age or coin the name Indus Valley Civilisation, so he cannot be credited with introducing the term.

 

• R. D. Banerjee (Option 3): R. D. Banerjee excavated Mohenjo-daro in 1922 on Marshall's instructions. He is credited with that excavation and not with proposing the term IVC for the whole culture.

 

• N. G. Majumdar (Option 4): N. G. Majumdar discovered Chanhudaro in 1931 on the Indus. His name is linked to that single site and its craft production, not to naming the civilisation.

question:
Consider the following statements about the names of the Indus Valley Civilisation:

1. It was first called the 'Indus Valley Civilisation'.

2. The name was later shortened to 'Indus Civilisation' as sites were found far away from the Indus valley.

3. It is also called the 'Harappan Civilisation' after the site discovered first.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• All three statements are correct. The culture was first named the Indus Valley Civilisation; the name was shortened to Indus Civilisation as sites kept turning up far from the Indus valley; and it is also called the Harappan Civilisation after the first-discovered site (तीन नाम — सिंधु, हड़प्पा)

 

• The shortening of the name is a cause-and-effect point: sites such as Alamgirpur (Meerut, UP) in the east and Daimabad (Maharashtra) in the south lie well outside the Indus basin.

 

• Naming a culture after its type-site is standard archaeological practice, and Harappa, excavated by Daya Ram Sahani in 1921, was that type-site.

 

• Because all three statements are true, any option that drops even one of them is incomplete and therefore wrong.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Harappa lies in Punjab, Pakistan, on the bank of the Ravi.

 

• Manda (J&K) is the northernmost site and Sutkagendor (Baluchistan) the westernmost.

 

• Alamgirpur on the Hindon is the easternmost and Daimabad on the Pravara the southernmost site.

 

• The PYQ 'IVC is also known as Harappan Civilization' (answer: Harappan) tests the same idea.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 1): This option leaves out statement 3, which is also correct. The civilisation is indeed called the Harappan Civilisation after Harappa, the site discovered first, so an answer without it is incomplete.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 3): This option leaves out statement 1, which is also correct. The first name used for the culture was the Indus Valley Civilisation, so dropping it makes the option incomplete.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 4): This option leaves out statement 2, which is also correct. The name was shortened to Indus Civilisation because sites were found far from the Indus valley, so the option is incomplete.

question: Which of the following pairs of Harappan site and the river on whose bank it lies is NOT correctly matched?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Daimabad - Ganga.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Daimabad is in Maharashtra on the Pravara river, not on the Ganga, so the pairing 'Daimabad - Ganga' is the wrongly matched one; it is the southernmost site of the civilisation (दैमाबाद — प्रवरा नदी)

 

• The other three pairs are correct: Manda (northernmost, Jammu & Kashmir) lies on the Chenab, Sutkagendor (westernmost, Baluchistan) on the Dasht, and Alamgirpur (easternmost, Meerut, UP) on the Hindon.

 

• The question is built on the four extreme sites, a favourite SSC theme; knowing each site with its river and state solves such pairs quickly.

 

• A NOT-correct question needs you to find the single false pair, so checking each pair against the notes is the right strategy.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Northernmost Manda, westernmost Sutkagendor, easternmost Alamgirpur, southernmost Daimabad.

 

• The Hindon is a tributary of the Yamuna in western Uttar Pradesh; the Ganga does not pass near Daimabad.

 

• Daimabad is also famous for a hoard of bronze objects.

 

• A PYQ asked the state of Daimabad (Maharashtra) and of Alamgirpur (Uttar Pradesh).

 

NOTE

 

• Manda - Chenab (Option 2): This pair is correct, so it is not the answer. Manda, the northernmost site, is in Jammu and Kashmir on the bank of the Chenab river, exactly as the notes state.

 

• Sutkagendor - Dasht (Option 3): This pair is correct, so it is not the answer. Sutkagendor, the westernmost site in Baluchistan, Pakistan, lies on the Dasht river, as the notes record.

 

• Alamgirpur - Hindon (Option 4): This pair is correct, so it is not the answer. Alamgirpur, the easternmost site near Meerut in Uttar Pradesh, stands on the bank of the Hindon river.

question:
Match the Harappan sites in Column I with their position/state in Column II.

Column I: (a) Manda  (b) Sutkagendor  (c) Alamgirpur  (d) Daimabad

Column II: (i) Southernmost site, Maharashtra  (ii) Northernmost site, Jammu & Kashmir  (iii) Westernmost site, Baluchistan  (iv) Easternmost site, Meerut (UP)
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct matching is Manda-ii (northernmost, Jammu and Kashmir), Sutkagendor-iii (westernmost, Baluchistan), Alamgirpur-iv (easternmost, Meerut, UP) and Daimabad-i (southernmost, Maharashtra), i.e. a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i (चरम सीमा के स्थल)

 

• These boundary sites show the vast spread of the civilisation from the Himalayan foothills to the Godavari-Pravara region and from Baluchistan to the Ganga-Yamuna doab.

 

• Memory aid: Manda = North, Sutkagendor = West, Alamgirpur = East, Daimabad = South; the matching options differ only in swapping these directions.

 

• Each site also has a river anchor: Chenab, Dasht, Hindon and Pravara respectively.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sutkagendor was explored by Aurel Stein and lies near the Makran coast.

 

• Alamgirpur is in the Ganga-Yamuna doab, in Meerut district.

 

• Daimabad is in Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra.

 

• Shortughai and Mundigak in Afghanistan are two other important sites.

 

• Sutkagendor was explored by Aurel Stein, and its position near the Makran coast links the civilisation with sea routes to the west; Manda, in Jammu district, lies at the foot of the Pir Panjal hills.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv (Option 1): This option swaps the directions of Manda and Sutkagendor and also of Alamgirpur and Daimabad. Manda is the northernmost site, not the westernmost, so the whole pairing collapses.

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii (Option 2): This option gets Manda right but wrongly makes Sutkagendor the southernmost site and Daimabad the westernmost. In reality Sutkagendor in Baluchistan is the westernmost and Daimabad in Maharashtra is the southernmost.

 

• a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i (Option 4): This option wrongly makes Manda the easternmost and Alamgirpur the northernmost site. Manda in Jammu and Kashmir is the northernmost, while Alamgirpur near Meerut in Uttar Pradesh is the easternmost, so the pairing is incorrect.

question:
Assertion (A): The Indus Valley Civilisation is called an urban civilisation.

Reason (R): Its towns were planned on a grid system with streets crossing at right angles and had underground drainage.

Select the correct option:
option_1: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true, but R is false
option_4: A is false, but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both A and R are true and R explains A: the IVC is called an urban civilisation because it was a civilisation of cities, and the evidence is the grid-based town planning, streets cutting at right angles, brick houses and an underground drainage system (नगरीय सभ्यता)

 

• Every house was linked to street drains covered with stone slabs or bricks, which implies municipal planning and civic control, the real marks of urbanism.

 

• Towns were also divided into a citadel on higher ground and a lower town, showing functional zoning.

 

• In assertion-reason questions, always test whether R is the cause or support of A; here planning and drainage are exactly why the culture is classed as urban.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• It was India's first civilisation, dated 2500-1750 BCE in the notes.

 

• Roads were of beaten earth and the grid was followed everywhere.

 

• Dholavira had three divisions and Chanhudaro no citadel.

 

• A PYQ asked which feature is NOT part of Indus cities: extensive iron tools.

 

• Contrast the Harappan towns with the contemporary village cultures of the Chalcolithic age in the rest of India, which had no planned streets, citadels, drains or large public buildings.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): This option would be wrong only if R were unrelated to A, but it is not: grid planning and drainage are the very reasons the civilisation is classed as urban, so R does explain A.

 

• A is true, but R is false (Option 3): This option would apply only if R were true but unconnected. Here R directly supports A, because planned streets and covered drains are core proofs of urban life, so it is not correct.

 

• A is false, but R is true (Option 4): This option claims R is false, but the grid pattern, right-angle roads and underground covered drains are all well-attested Harappan features, so R is true.

question: Which of the following was NOT a feature of Harappan cities?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Extensive use of iron tools.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Harappan cities did not use iron at all; iron was unknown to the Harappans, who worked gold, copper, tin, bronze, silver and lead, so extensive use of iron tools is the feature that does NOT belong (लोहे का अज्ञान)

 

• The cities did show a grid pattern, with streets crossing at almost perfect right angles into rectangular blocks, and a lower town of brick houses below the citadel.

 

• Drains were underground and covered with stone slabs or bricks, and every house was connected to them.

 

• This is a standard 'NOT a feature' type question; the safe approach is to eliminate the planning features and pick the technological anachronism, iron.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Copper came from the Khetri mines of Rajasthan, and tin was alloyed to make bronze.

 

• Iron appeared in the Gangetic plain around 1000 BCE.

 

• A PYQ asked the same idea: the Harappans belonged to the Bronze Age, so iron tools were not a characteristic.

 

• A similar PYQ listed 'use of iron' as NOT a feature of the Neolithic period.

 

NOTE

 

• Grid pattern of streets (Option 2): The grid pattern was a real Harappan feature, so it cannot be the answer. Streets met almost exactly at right angles and cut the city into rectangular blocks.

 

• Underground drains covered with slabs (Option 3): Covered underground drains were a real feature, so this is not the answer. Each house was connected to street drains covered with stone slabs or bricks.

 

• Lower town of brick houses (Option 4): The lower town of brick houses was a real feature, so it is not the answer. Ordinary people lived there below the citadel on the eastern side.

question: What was the material used for making roads in the Harappan towns?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Beaten earth.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• As per the notes, the material used for the Harappan roads was beaten earth, whereas the drains running beside the houses were covered with stone slabs or bricks (कुटी हुई मिट्टी की सड़कें)

 

• The roads were laid in a grid and met at nearly 90 degree right angles, so even though the surface was earthen the layout was highly planned.

 

• Houses and public buildings, by contrast, were built with burnt bricks, which should not be confused with the road surface.

 

• Be careful with the word 'bitumen': it was used to waterproof the Great Bath, not for roads.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Bitumen (natural tar) waterproofed the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro.

 

• The Harappan brick was standard-sized and burnt, as a PYQ notes (burnt mud-bricks).

 

• Cities were enclosed by fortified walls with gateways, another PYQ point.

 

• Uniformity of the grid pattern is seen across sites.

 

• Compare roads and drains: the roads were of beaten earth, the drains beside them were covered with stone slabs or bricks, and the houses were of burnt brick, so each element had its own material.

 

NOTE

 

• Stone slabs (Option 1): Stone slabs were used to cover some drains, not to surface the roads. The notes clearly state that roads were made of beaten earth, so this option confuses drain covers with road material.

 

• Baked bricks (Option 2): Baked bricks were used for houses, drains and bathing platforms, but the roads themselves were beaten earth. This option mixes up the building material with the road surface.

 

• Bitumen (Option 3): Bitumen was a natural tar used for waterproofing the Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro. It was never the road-making material, so this option confuses a waterproofing agent with road surface.

question:
Consider the following statements about Harappan drainage:

1. Every house was connected to the street drains.

2. The drains were covered with stone slabs or bricks.

3. The drainage system was above ground and open.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The Harappan underground drainage system connected every house to street drains, which were covered with stone slabs or bricks; statement 3 is false because the drains were not above ground and open (भूमिगत जल निकास प्रणाली)

 

• The drains were a striking feature of Harappan town planning and show a sense of public sanitation and civic organisation.

 

• As a PYQ answer explains, the drainage system was highly advanced and available to the general population, not only to the royal class.

 

• An exception in the notes is Banawali, where no drainage system was found, which shows that the covered drain was the general norm but not universal.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Dholavira, in contrast, is famous for its water harvesting with a reservoir and dam.

 

• Mohenjo-daro had the most advanced drainage, as per a PYQ.

 

• The Great Bath was waterproofed with bitumen.

 

• Roads were of beaten earth.

 

• In everyday terms the covered drains worked like a modern sewer line: household waste flowed into street drains, which prevented stagnation and reflected strong municipal control in the large cities.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): This option takes statement 3 as true and drops statement 1. The drains were underground and covered, not above ground and open, and every house was connected to them, so statement 1 is correct.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): This option takes statement 3 as true and drops statement 2. The drains were covered with stone slabs or bricks, so they were not open, which makes statement 3 false.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): This option includes all three, but statement 3 is false because the system was underground and covered, so choosing every statement is incorrect.

question:
Consider the following statements regarding Harappan town planning:

1. The citadel stood on the western side on higher ground.

2. The lower town lay on the eastern side at a lower level.

3. The citadel was inhabited by the poor.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The citadel stood on the western, higher side of the town, while the lower town lay on the eastern, lower side; statement 3 is wrong because the citadel was meant for the rich/ruling elite, not the poor (दुर्ग पश्चिम, निचला नगर पूर्व)

 

• Below the citadel lay the lower town, with brick houses where the ordinary people lived.

 

• Nearly every site followed this plan; the notes list two exceptions: Dholavira (Citadel, Middle town and Lower town) and Chanhudaro (no citadel).

 

• Remember the pair of ideas 'west-high-rich' and 'east-low-poor'; reversing them is the usual trap.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The same two-part pattern held at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro.

 

• Dholavira alone had a three-part layout.

 

• Chanhudaro had no citadel and was a craft-production town.

 

• A PYQ asked the shape of Harappan cities: rectangular grid.

 

• Citadel mounds were raised on platforms and held public buildings, which is why the western mound at sites like Harappa and Mohenjo-daro is often described as the seat of the rulers.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 (Option 1): This option takes only statement 1 and leaves out statement 2. The lower town did lie on the eastern side at a lower level, so statement 2 is also correct and this answer is incomplete.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): This option includes statement 3 and omits statement 1. The citadel was meant for the rich and not for the poor, so statement 3 is false and statement 1 is correct.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): This option includes all three statements, but statement 3 is false. The citadel on higher ground was for the rich, while the poor lived in the lower town.

question: Which Harappan site is unique in being divided into three parts - the Citadel, the Middle town and the Lower town?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dholavira.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Dholavira is the only Harappan site divided into three parts: the Citadel, the Middle town and the Lower town, whereas nearly every other site had just a citadel and a lower town (धौलावीरा — तीन भागों में विभाजित)

 

• It lies at Khadir Bet (Khadir island) in the Rann of Kutch, Gujarat, in a semi-arid zone, which explains its famous water management system with a big reservoir and a dam.

 

• It was discovered by J. P. Joshi in 1967-68, and large-scale excavation began in 1990 under R. S. Bisht.

 

• UNESCO included Dholavira in the World Heritage List in 2021, so it is a favourite for current-affairs-linked history questions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Dholavira is known for its stone fortifications, as a PYQ answer notes.

 

• Chanhudaro, in contrast, had no citadel at all.

 

• Surkotada, also in the Rann of Kutch, was found by J. P. Joshi in 1964.

 

• Most other sites followed the two-part citadel and lower-town plan.

 

• Dholavira's Citadel, Middle town and Lower town were separated by walls, and the site is also known for a large signboard with ten big Indus signs, a rare case of readable-size lettering.

 

NOTE

 

• Lothal (Option 2): Lothal followed the usual two-part plan and is famous for the only artificial dockyard and for carnelian bead-making, not for a three-part layout.

 

• Kalibangan (Option 3): Kalibangan had the usual citadel and lower-town plan; it is known for seven fire altars and the ploughed field with criss-cross furrows.

 

• Harappa (Option 4): Harappa followed the standard citadel and lower-town arrangement and is known for its granary of 12 units, not for a middle town.

question: Which is the only Harappan site that had no citadel and was devoted entirely to craft production?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Chanhudaro.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Chanhudaro in Sindh, Pakistan, is the only IVC site with no citadel; the place was devoted entirely to craft production, and a bead-making factory was found there (चन्हूदड़ो — बिना दुर्ग का शिल्प नगर)

 

• It was discovered by N. G. Majumdar in 1931 on the bank of the Indus.

 

• A terracotta model of a bullock cart was also found, which hints at transport of goods between craft centres and markets.

 

• The absence of a citadel makes Chanhudaro the usual exception to the citadel-lower town plan, alongside Dholavira's three-part layout.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Carnelian beads were produced at Chanhudaro and Lothal.

 

• A PYQ describes Chanhudaro as a craft production centre while Lothal had a dockyard.

 

• Bead-making is Chanhudaro's signature as another PYQ shows.

 

• Mohenjo-daro is only a short distance away in Sindh.

 

• Because Chanhudaro lacked a citadel and specialised in crafts, historians see it as a production centre that supplied beads and other goods to the larger cities and, through them, to overseas buyers.

 

NOTE

 

• Banawali (Option 1): Banawali in Hisar, Haryana, had a citadel-lower town structure; it is known for a terracotta plough model and for lacking a drainage system, not for being citadel-less.

 

• Surkotada (Option 2): Surkotada in the Rann of Kutch, found by J. P. Joshi in 1964, had a fortified citadel; it is not the craft town without a citadel.

 

• Rakhigarhi (Option 3): Rakhigarhi in Haryana is the biggest IVC site inside India and had a normal town structure; it is not devoted entirely to craft production.

question:
Match the Harappan sites in Column I with the rivers in Column II.

Column I: (a) Harappa  (b) Mohenjo-daro  (c) Rakhigarhi  (d) Alamgirpur

Column II: (i) Hindon  (ii) Ravi  (iii) Ghaggar  (iv) Indus
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Harappa lies on the Ravi, Mohenjo-daro on the Indus, Rakhigarhi on the Ghaggar and Alamgirpur on the Hindon, so the correct matching is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i (हड़प्पा-रावी, मोहनजोदड़ो-सिंधु)

 

• Harappa, in Punjab (Pakistan), gave the civilisation its second name; Mohenjo-daro at Larkana in Sindh is the largest city.

 

• Rakhigarhi, in Hisar, Haryana, is the biggest IVC site inside India, while Alamgirpur in Meerut is the easternmost site.

 

• River-site matching is a high-frequency theme; the safe approach is to anchor the most certain pair first, such as Harappa-Ravi, and eliminate options.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Chanhudaro is also on the Indus; Kalibangan lies in the Ghaggar basin in Rajasthan.

 

• Daimabad lies on the Pravara; Manda on the Chenab; Sutkagendor on the Dasht.

 

• A PYQ confirms that Harappa was found on the bank of the Ravi.

 

• The Ghaggar is often linked with the Saraswati by many scholars.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii (Option 1): This option gives the Indus to Harappa and the Ravi to Mohenjo-daro, which reverses the correct pair. It also mismatches Rakhigarhi with the Hindon and Alamgirpur with the Ghaggar.

 

• a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii (Option 3): This option correctly gives the Indus to Mohenjo-daro but wrongly pairs Rakhigarhi with the Hindon and Alamgirpur with the Ghaggar. Rakhigarhi is on the Ghaggar and Alamgirpur on the Hindon.

 

• a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i (Option 4): This option assigns the Ghaggar to Harappa and the Ravi to Rakhigarhi, which is wrong. Harappa stands on the Ravi and Rakhigarhi on the Ghaggar.

question: The Harappan site of Harappa, excavated in 1921 by Daya Ram Sahani, is located on the bank of which river?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ravi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Harappa, lying in Punjab, Pakistan, was excavated in 1921 by Daya Ram Sahani on the bank of the Ravi river (हड़प्पा — रावी नदी)

 

• Daya Ram Sahani was sent to the Sindhu region by John Marshall, the Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India.

 

• Because Harappa was the first site found, the whole culture is also called the Harappan Civilisation.

 

• Hence, when a question mentions Harappa and 1921 together, the river is the Ravi; the Indus is for Mohenjo-daro and Chanhudaro.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• SSC has previously asked the very same river for Harappa (answer: Ravi).

 

• The biggest building at Harappa was a granary of 12 units in two rows of six.

 

• Mohenjo-daro was excavated in 1922 by R. D. Banerjee.

 

• Harappa is in present-day Pakistan.

 

• The Ravi is one of the five rivers of Punjab and a tributary of the Chenab; the Harappan town stood on its old bank before the river changed its course.

 

NOTE

 

• Indus (Option 1): The Indus is the river of Mohenjo-daro and Chanhudaro. Harappa stands on the Ravi, so this option confuses the civilisation's main river with the river of the site.

 

• Sutlej (Option 2): The Sutlej is not linked with Harappa in the notes. Harappa lies on the Ravi, so the Sutlej is a plausible but wrong Punjab river.

 

• Chenab (Option 3): The Chenab is the river on which Manda, the northernmost site in Jammu and Kashmir, is situated. It is not the river of Harappa.

question: Which was the biggest building found at Harappa, consisting of 12 units arranged in two rows of six?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Granary.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The biggest building at Harappa was a granary with 12 units arranged in two rows of six; a row of six granaries is also noted at the site (अन्नागार — हड़प्पा)

 

• Large granaries point to a state-level organisation that collected and stored surplus wheat and barley, the two main crops.

 

• Harappa lies in Punjab, Pakistan, on the Ravi, and was excavated by Daya Ram Sahani in 1921.

 

• Other finds mentioned for Harappa are a statue of a woman and a dice.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mohenjo-daro's largest building is also described as a granary.

 

• A PYQ on circular platforms at Harappa says they were used for threshing grain, not for religious ceremonies.

 

• Wheat and barley grains were found there.

 

• Granaries stood in the citadel area.

 

• Granaries stored surplus grain collected from farmers, so large storage buildings in the citadel suggest an organised authority that handled revenue or rations in kind, since the Harappans used no coins.

 

NOTE

 

• Great Bath (Option 2): The Great Bath is the most important public structure of Mohenjo-daro, not Harappa, and it is a water tank rather than a building of 12 units arranged in two rows.

 

• Dockyard (Option 3): The dockyard is a feature of Lothal in Gujarat, a coastal trade site. It is the only artificial dockyard, and it has nothing to do with the 12-unit building at Harappa.

 

• Fire altar (Option 4): Fire altars, seven in number, were found at Kalibangan in Rajasthan. They are ritual structures and are not a big building of 12 units at Harappa.

question:
Match the Harappan sites in Column I with their excavators/discoverers in Column II.

Column I: (a) Harappa  (b) Mohenjo-daro  (c) Chanhudaro  (d) Banawali

Column II: (i) R. D. Banerjee  (ii) Daya Ram Sahani  (iii) N. G. Majumdar  (iv) R. S. Bisht
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Harappa was excavated by Daya Ram Sahani (1921), Mohenjo-daro by R. D. Banerjee (1922), Chanhudaro by N. G. Majumdar (1931) and Banawali by R. S. Bisht (1973-74), giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv (उत्खननकर्ता)

 

• The chronological order of discovery (1921, 1922, 1931) is a useful memory device because Harappa and Mohenjo-daro are often interchanged.

 

• Banawali, in Hisar, Haryana, is a Haryana site; its excavator R. S. Bisht later led the large-scale excavations at Dholavira.

 

• Match-the-following questions of this type are usually solved by fixing the two certain pairs, Harappa-Sahani and Mohenjo-daro-Banerjee.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Lothal was discovered by S. R. Rao (1954-55) and Surkotada by J. P. Joshi (1964).

 

• Dholavira was found by J. P. Joshi (1967-68) and excavated from 1990 by R. S. Bisht.

 

• John Marshall directed the ASI and sent Sahani to the Indus region.

 

• Kalibangan lies in Rajasthan; Rakhigarhi in Haryana.

 

NOTE

 

• a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv (Option 1): This option swaps Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, giving Banerjee to Harappa and Sahani to Mohenjo-daro. Harappa was Sahani's excavation (1921) and Mohenjo-daro Banerjee's (1922).

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii (Option 3): This option has Harappa and Mohenjo-daro right but swaps Chanhudaro and Banawali. N. G. Majumdar found Chanhudaro in 1931 and R. S. Bisht found Banawali in 1973-74.

 

• a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv (Option 4): This option gives Harappa to N. G. Majumdar and Chanhudaro to Sahani, which are both wrong. Majumdar discovered Chanhudaro, while Sahani excavated Harappa.

question: What is the literal meaning of 'Mohenjo-daro', as the site is known?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mount of Dead.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mohenjo-daro is known as the 'Mount (Mound) of Dead' because the highest number of skeletons was recovered from this site (मोहनजोदड़ो — मृतकों का टीला)

 

• It is situated at Larkana in Sindh, Pakistan, on the bank of the Indus, and was excavated by R. D. Banerjee in 1922.

 

• It is the largest of all the Indus cities, and its most important public structure is the Great Bath.

 

• Do not confuse the meaning of the name with its famous features such as the Great Bath or granary.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• A bronze dancing girl and a steatite bearded man were found here; a PYQ confirms the bearded man at Mohenjo-daro.

 

• The Pashupati seal is from here.

 

• UNESCO listed Mohenjo-daro as a World Heritage Site in 1980.

 

• A PYQ describes it as containing a Great Granary and showing evidence of repeated floods.

 

NOTE

 

• City of Bath (Option 2): The Great Bath is a structure found inside the city; the name Mohenjo-daro does not mean 'City of Bath'. Choosing it mixes up the monument with the meaning of the name.

 

• Mound of Granaries (Option 3): Granaries were found at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, but the name does not mean 'Mound of Granaries'. It refers to the large number of skeletons recovered.

 

• Abode of Craftsmen (Option 4): Chanhudaro, not Mohenjo-daro, was the craft-production town. 'Abode of Craftsmen' is not the meaning of the name, which refers to the dead.

question: Which material was used to make the Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro waterproof?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bitumen.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• To make the Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro waterproof, bitumen (natural tar) was used, which sealed the brickwork against leakage (विशाल स्नानागार — बिटुमिन)

 

• The Great Bath is the most important public structure at Mohenjo-daro, a large rectangular tank, believed to have been used for ritual bathing.

 

• It is made of burnt bricks and its watertight lining shows the engineering skill of the Harappans.

 

• Mohenjo-daro lies at Larkana in Sindh and was excavated by R. D. Banerjee in 1922.

 

• Bitumen is a natural tar that occurs in the Indus-Mesopotamia region, and its use on the Great Bath also hints at links with Mesopotamian building practice.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The tank is roughly 12 m long, 7 m wide and 2.4 m deep.

 

• A PYQ asked what the Great Bath is known for: a large rectangular tank.

 

• Another PYQ asked its site: Mohenjo-daro.

 

• The largest building at Mohenjo-daro is a granary.

 

• The Great Bath was about 12 m long, 7 m wide and 2.4 m deep, with steps at both ends and surrounding rooms, which supports the view that it was used for ritual or ceremonial bathing.

 

NOTE

 

• Lime plaster (Option 1): Lime plaster is a mortar of later building traditions. The notes say the Great Bath was made waterproof with bitumen, a natural tar, so lime plaster is a plausible but wrong choice.

 

• Gypsum (Option 3): Gypsum mortar is not mentioned for the Great Bath. The waterproofing agent was bitumen (natural tar), so gypsum is a distractor that sounds technical but is incorrect.

 

• Lead sheets (Option 4): Lead was known to the Harappans as a metal, but sheets of lead were not what made the Great Bath watertight. The material used was bitumen.

question:
Consider the following statements about Mohenjo-daro:

1. It is situated at Larkana in Sindh, Pakistan.

2. R. D. Banerjee excavated it in 1922 on the bank of the Indus.

3. It is the smallest of all the Indus cities.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statements 1 and 2 are correct; statement 3 is false because Mohenjo-daro is the largest of all the Indus cities, not the smallest (मोहनजोदड़ो — सबसे बड़ा नगर)

 

• It lies at Larkana in Sindh, Pakistan, and was excavated by R. D. Banerjee in 1922 on the bank of the Indus.

 

• It is called the 'Mount of Dead' because the highest number of skeletons was found there, and it has the Great Bath and a granary.

 

• The word 'smallest' in a statement about a famous city should immediately raise suspicion.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rakhigarhi is the biggest IVC site inside India, while Mohenjo-daro is the largest overall.

 

• Harappa was excavated a year earlier, in 1921.

 

• The bronze dancing girl and steatite bearded man are from Mohenjo-daro.

 

• The Pashupati seal comes from this site.

 

• Mohenjo-daro was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980; its Great Bath and its covered drains are the structures most often cited as proof of Harappan engineering.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): This option accepts statement 3 and rejects statement 1. Larkana in Sindh is indeed the location of Mohenjo-daro, so statement 1 is correct and statement 3 is false.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): This option accepts statement 3 and rejects statement 2. R. D. Banerjee did excavate Mohenjo-daro in 1922 on the Indus bank, so statement 2 is true, while the claim of 'smallest' is false.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): This option accepts all three, but statement 3 is false. Mohenjo-daro was the largest and not the smallest of all the Indus cities.

question: The bronze figure of a dancing girl, admired for its craftsmanship, was found at which site?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mohenjo-daro.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The bronze dancing girl, admired for its craftsmanship, was found at Mohenjo-daro, together with the steatite image of a bearded man (stone sculpture) (कांस्य नर्तकी — मोहनजोदड़ो)

 

• The figurine shows the Harappans' skill in bronze casting, since bronze is an alloy of copper and tin.

 

• Mohenjo-daro in Sindh is the largest Indus city and also yielded the famous Pashupati seal.

 

• These finds are standard SSC association questions; learn site-find pairs together.

 

• Because a bronze statue needs copper and tin, such a figurine also reminds us that metal supplies came from the Khetri mines and from trade with far regions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• A PYQ asked where the stone sculpture of a bearded man was found: Mohenjo-daro.

 

• Mohenjo-daro's Great Bath is its other major find.

 

• Mohenjo-daro was excavated by R. D. Banerjee in 1922.

 

• The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

 

• The figurine is about 10 cm high, shows a young woman with bangles on one arm, and was probably made by the lost-wax method, which shows advanced metalworking skill.

 

NOTE

 

• Chanhudaro (Option 2): Chanhudaro is known for a bead-making factory and a terracotta model of a bullock cart. It is a craft-production town and not the findspot of the bronze dancing girl.

 

• Kalibangan (Option 3): Kalibangan is known for seven fire altars and a ploughed field with criss-cross furrows, not for the bronze dancing girl found at Mohenjo-daro.

 

• Banawali (Option 4): Banawali is known for a terracotta plough model and the absence of a drainage system. It is unconnected with the bronze dancing girl.

question: Where was 'carnelian', a stone used by the Harappans for making beads, mostly found?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Gujarat.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Carnelian, a stone used by the Harappans for making beads, was mostly found in Gujarat, at sites such as Lothal and Chanhudaro, where bead-making was an important craft (कार्नेलियन — गुजरात)

 

• A PYQ explanation adds that the stone was mainly obtained from Gujarat, especially the Khambhat (Cambay) region.

 

• Chanhudaro in Sindh had a bead-making factory, and finished beads were traded to far regions like Mesopotamia.

 

• The question is a direct factual one, repeated in the PYQ bank, so link carnelian with Gujarat firmly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Beads, seals and metal goods were the typical craft products of the Harappan towns.

 

• Lothal in Gujarat combined bead-making with its role as a port through the dockyard.

 

• Foreign trade partners included Mesopotamia, Afghanistan and Iran, where beads travelled.

 

• Gujarat also holds Dholavira and Surkotada in the Rann of Kutch.

 

NOTE

 

• Assam (Option 1): Assam is not a source of carnelian for the Harappans and lies far from the Harappan zone. The notes link the stone with Gujarat, so choosing Assam relies on guesswork about north-east India.

 

• Punjab (Option 2): Punjab holds Harappa, but the notes tie carnelian to Gujarat, with Lothal and Chanhudaro as bead-making centres. A major city region need not be the source of a raw stone.

 

• Bihar (Option 3): Bihar was outside the Harappan heartland and is not linked with carnelian in the notes. The stone was mostly found in Gujarat, so Bihar is incorrect.

question: Which pair of Harappan sites was discovered by J. P. Joshi?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Surkotada and Dholavira.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• According to the notes, J. P. Joshi discovered Surkotada (1964, Rann of Kutch, Gujarat) and Dholavira (Khadir Bet, Rann of Kutch), so the pair is Surkotada and Dholavira (जे. पी. जोशी)

 

• Dholavira was found by Joshi in 1967-68, and large-scale excavation began only in 1990 under R. S. Bisht, which is why some books mention 1990-91.

 

• Both sites lie in the Rann of Kutch, a clue that helps link the two names with one discoverer.

 

• Dholavira is the only site divided into three parts, and Surkotada is one of the Kutch sites of the civilisation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Lothal was discovered by S. R. Rao (1954-55), a Gujarat site far from the Kutch pair.

 

• Banawali was discovered by R. S. Bisht (1973-74) at Hisar in Haryana.

 

• Chanhudaro was found by N. G. Majumdar in 1931 in Sindh.

 

• Remember the discoverer groups: Joshi - Kutch sites; Bisht - Haryana site; Majumdar - Sindh site.

 

NOTE

 

• Lothal and Kalibangan (Option 1): Lothal was discovered by S. R. Rao and Kalibangan lies in Rajasthan, so the pair does not belong to Joshi. This option mixes sites of two different archaeologists.

 

• Banawali and Rakhigarhi (Option 2): Banawali was found by R. S. Bisht in Haryana, and Rakhigarhi is also a Haryana site. Neither is a Joshi discovery, so the pair is incorrect.

 

• Harappa and Chanhudaro (Option 4): Harappa was excavated by Daya Ram Sahani in 1921 and Chanhudaro by N. G. Majumdar in 1931. Neither was discovered by J. P. Joshi.

question: Why was the Harappan site of Kalibangan given its name?
option_1: Seven fire altars were found here
option_4: Black bangles were dug up here
solution_text:
The correct answer is Black bangles were dug up here.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The name Kalibangan (kali + bangan, 'black bangles') was given because black bangles were dug up at the site (कालीबंगा — काली चूड़ियाँ)

 

• It lies in Ganganagar district (renamed Hanumangarh), Rajasthan, in the Ghaggar region.

 

• Its famous finds are 7 fire altars, a ploughed field together with a wooden furrow, and criss-cross plough marks in fields.

 

• Learning the origin of the name is a classic one-line trick: black bangles = Kalibangan.

 

• The name is a local Rajasthani place-name meaning black bangles, and has nothing to do with the Harappans' own name for the town, which is unknown to us.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• A PYQ asked which agricultural evidence was found at Kalibangan: criss-cross plough marks in fields.

 

• Fire altars at Kalibangan suggest ritual practice even though no temple has been found in the IVC.

 

• Wheat and barley were the main crops, and sesame, mustard and cotton were also grown.

 

• Banawali yielded only a terracotta model of a plough, unlike Kalibangan's real field.

 

NOTE

 

• Seven fire altars were found here (Option 1): Seven fire altars were indeed found at Kalibangan, but the name comes from the black bangles dug up there. The altars are a famous find and not the origin of the name.

 

• Dockyard was found here (Option 2): The dockyard belongs to Lothal in Gujarat and has no connection with Kalibangan or its name. Choosing it confuses two sites on the basis of one frequent fact.

 

• Bead-making factory was found here (Option 3): The bead-making factory was found at Chanhudaro in Sindh. It is a craft-production find and not the reason for the name Kalibangan.

question:
Consider the following statements about Kalibangan:

1. Seven fire altars were found here.

2. A ploughed field with a wooden furrow was discovered here.

3. An artificial dockyard was found here.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statements 1 and 2 hold true: Kalibangan yielded 7 fire altars and a ploughed field with a wooden furrow and criss-cross plough marks; statement 3 is wrong because the artificial dockyard is at Lothal (कालीबंगा — अग्निवेदियाँ, जुता खेत)

 

• The ploughed field is direct evidence of Harappan agriculture, and a PYQ answer calls the criss-cross furrows the earliest archaeological evidence of a ploughed field.

 

• Fire altars suggest ritual practice, although the notes stress that no temple has ever been found.

 

• Do not confuse this with Banawali, where only a terracotta model of a plough was found.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kalibangan is in Hanumangarh (formerly Ganganagar), Rajasthan, so it is not a Gujarat site.

 

• Its name arose from black bangles dug up at the site.

 

• The dockyard belongs to Lothal, whose S. R. Rao excavations are separate from Kalibangan.

 

• A PYQ treated the pair 'Kalibangan - fire altars' as correct.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 (Option 2): This option picks only statement 1 and ignores statement 2. The ploughed field with a wooden furrow was also found at Kalibangan, so the option is incomplete.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 3): This option includes statement 3 and omits statement 1. The dockyard is not at Kalibangan, while the seven fire altars certainly are, so it is incorrect.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): This option includes all three statements, but statement 3 is false. The only artificial dockyard of the civilisation was at Lothal, not Kalibangan.

question: Kalibangan, a Harappan site famous for its fire altars, is located in which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rajasthan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Kalibangan is in Ganganagar district (name changed to Hanumangarh) of Rajasthan, on the Ghaggar region plain (कालीबंगा — राजस्थान)

 

• It is best known for seven fire altars, a ploughed field and criss-cross plough marks, and its name comes from the black bangles found there.

 

• Rajasthan is also the state of the Khetri mines, from which the Harappans obtained copper.

 

• Keeping the state-wise list straight is useful: Rajasthan - Kalibangan; Haryana - Rakhigarhi, Banawali; Gujarat - Lothal, Dholavira, Surkotada.

 

• The Ghaggar region plain on which the site stands is the Rajasthan part of the old Ghaggar-Hakra valley, where many Harappan settlements are found.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• SSC has previously asked the state of Rakhigarhi, and the answer was Haryana.

 

• Daimabad lies in Maharashtra and Alamgirpur in Uttar Pradesh, both frequent PYQ items.

 

• Harappa and Mohenjo-daro are in Pakistan, in Punjab and Sindh respectively.

 

• Manda, the northernmost site, is in Jammu and Kashmir.

 

• Fire altars and ploughed fields at Kalibangan were excavated by B. B. Lal and B. K. Thapar in the 1960s, after A. Ghosh had first noticed the site in 1953.

 

NOTE

 

• Gujarat (Option 1): Gujarat has Lothal, Dholavira and Surkotada, not Kalibangan. It is a frequent trap because Gujarat has the most coastal and Kutch sites of the civilisation.

 

• Haryana (Option 2): Haryana has Rakhigarhi and Banawali in Hisar region, but not Kalibangan. The two states are neighbours, which is why they are mixed up.

 

• Punjab (Option 3): The Punjab region of Pakistan holds Harappa on the Ravi river. Kalibangan lies in Hanumangarh district of Rajasthan, so choosing Punjab confuses the state with the Pakistani province.
